intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that early-onset dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia (DYTSPG) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP5MC3 gene (602736) on chromosome 2q31.

checks.claim: Early-onset dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia (DYTSPG) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP5MC3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: A unique form of familial spastic paraplegia and dystonia is associated with a heterozygous ATP5MC3 variant that also reduces mitochondrial complex V activity.
checks.explanation: The paper links a heterozygous ATP5MC3 variant to dystonia and spastic paraplegia.

checks.claim: The ATP5MC3 gene is located on chromosome 2q31.
checks.evidence_quote: linkage analysis previously mapped the disease to chromosome 2q24-2q31.
checks.explanation: The gene lies in the mapped 2q24-q31 region. Giving the gene's standard cytogenetic location (2q31) is acceptable nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Early-onset dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia is an autosomal dominant neurologic disorder. Its presentation varies, even within one family. Some affected individuals have childhood-onset, progressive dystonia that may generalize. Others have later-onset focal limb or neck dystonia or spasmodic dysphonia. Still others have gradually progressive spastic paraplegia that begins in adulthood (Neilson et al., 2022). Some patients also have developmental delay or intellectual disability (Zech et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Gilbert et al. (2009) reported a large multigenerational kindred from Ohio with a highly penetrant autosomal dominant neurologic disorder causing spasticity and dystonia. Spasticity and weakness began anywhere from the first year of life to the sixth decade, and dystonia began between the first and third decades. Affected members had no ataxia and no apparent cognitive involvement. Neuroimaging and peripheral neurophysiology were normal.

paragraphs.text: Neilson et al. (2022) summarized a large multigenerational family (Family-1) segregating autosomal dominant dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia. Of 40 individuals in the pedigree, 18 were affected. They had either childhood-onset, progressive generalized dystonia or adult-onset, gradually progressive spastic paraplegia. Some members had less severe, later-onset focal limb and neck dystonia or spasmodic dysphonia. When performed, brain MRI and peripheral nerve physiology were normal. The proband developed unilateral upper limb dystonia at age 2 years. It generalized to the trunk and all limbs and caused loss of ambulation. His father and grandfather had the hereditary spastic paraplegia phenotype, with progressive leg weakness and spasticity beginning after age 20 years. Metabolic studies were normal in the proband and his father, including blood lactate and pyruvate, serum amino acids, urine organic acids, and acylcarnitine profiles.

Brain MRI showed nonspecific mild bilateral frontoparietal white matter changes.

paragraphs.text: Zech et al. (2022) described 3 unrelated patients with ATP5MC3 mutations. Patient 8, a previously reported 12-year-old boy, had isolated upper-limb dystonia. Patient 9, a 15-year-old girl, had a history of milestone delay, pyramidal signs, and generalized dystonia with prominent upper-body involvement. Patient 10, a 6-year-old boy, had delayed psychomotor development, lower-extremity spasticity, and elevated blood lactate. Zech et al. (2022) combined their 3 patients with the multigenerational family reported by Neilson et al. (2022). Across these 18 individuals, the disorder included dystonia in 12, spasticity or pyramidal signs in 17, and developmental delay or intellectual disability in 2. Ten individuals had dystonia-predominant syndromes. The authors noted that patients 9 and 10 confirmed spastic symptoms in independent families and added neurodevelopmental comorbidity to the phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Neilson et al. (2022) studied fibroblasts from the Family-1 proband, who had dystonia, and his affected father, who had hereditary spastic paraplegia. Activities of complexes I through IV were normal. Complex V activity was reduced by 20%, cellular ATP by 20 to 32%, and oxygen consumption by 21 to 25%. Oxygen consumption and ATP were reduced in proportion, so the authors did not consider uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation a likely mechanism.

A secondary analysis searched for candidate regions segregating with the dystonia phenotype and found 2 regions with parametric lod scores above 2.0.

paragraphs.text: Neilson et al. (2022) studied affected members of Family-1, whose disorder had previously been mapped to chromosome 2q24-q31. Using whole-exome sequencing restricted to the linkage region, they identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the ATP5MC3 gene (c.318C-G; asn106-to-lys, N106K). Sanger sequencing showed that only affected individuals carried the mutation. It was absent from gnomAD v2.1.1 and v3.1.1, affected a highly conserved loop that contacts the F1 subunit, and was predicted damaging by all in silico tools used. The authors concluded that ATP5MC3 remained the primary candidate for the spastic paraplegia in this family.

paragraphs.text: Zech et al. (2022) identified de novo heterozygous missense mutations in ATP5MC3 by whole-exome sequencing in 3 unrelated patients. The first, a 12-year-old boy with isolated upper-limb dystonia (patient 8), came from a cohort of 1,012 dystonia patients. He carried the N106K mutation, which had previously been identified in an independent pedigree with 18 of 40 members affected by dystonia and/or spasticity. His fibroblasts showed a slight but significant decrease in ATPase activity and a reduced oxygen consumption rate. paragraphs.text: Neilson et al. (2022) studied a large multigenerational family (Family-1) with autosomal dominant dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia. In affected members, they identified a heterozygous c.318C-G transversion in the ATP5MC3 gene, resulting in an asn106-to-lys (N106K) substitution. They found it by whole-exome sequencing restricted to the previously mapped linkage region on chromosome 2q24-q31. Sanger sequencing showed that only affected individuals carried the mutation. It was absent from gnomAD v2.1.1 and v3.1.1, affected a highly conserved loop that contacts the F1 subunit, and was predicted damaging by in silico tools. Fibroblasts from the proband and his affected father showed a 20% reduction in complex V activity, a 20 to 32% reduction in cellular ATP, and a 21 to 25% reduction in oxygen consumption. Activities of complexes I through IV were normal.
